t: Maximum Number of Items From Sale I — Knapsack Over Item Types
o:
You buy copies of items within a budget, then every **distinct item type** you bought at least one copy of grants one free copy of every other type whose factor it divides. Crucially, extra copies of a type give no extra free copies, so the free-copy bonus depends only on the *set* of types purchased, while the purchased-copy count depends on how many copies you buy.

**Example 1:** items = [[6,2],[2,6],[3,4]], budget = 9. Buying {item 0, item 2} costs 2+4=6 and yields 2 purchased copies plus 1 free copy (factor 3 divides 6) = 3, leaving 3 budget → one more copy of the cheapest item (price 2) → total 4.

**Example 2:** Buying one copy each of items 0,1,2 (cost 7) earns 1+2+1=4 free copies; with 1 budget left we buy another price-1 copy of item 2, totaling 5 purchased + 5 free = 10.

Constraints (n, factor, price, budget ≤ 1500) hint at an $O(n \cdot \text{budget})$ dynamic program: treat "buy at least one copy of type i" as a 0/1 choice worth `1 + cnt_i` (its own copy plus its free contributions), then spend all remaining budget on the globally cheapest item.
k: Free copies depend only on WHICH item types were bought (at least once), not how many copies — so each type contributes a fixed bonus 1 + cnt_i when first purchased.
Any leftover budget is best spent on the globally cheapest item, since duplicate purchases never increase the free-copy bonus.
This reduces the problem to a 0/1 knapsack: pick a set of types maximizing (count + free bonus) under a cost constraint, then add floor(remaining budget / min price).

a.i: Enumerate every subset of item types that could be bought (one copy each). For each subset compute its cost, its free-copy count from divisibility pairs, and fill leftover budget with copies of the cheapest item. This directly mirrors the problem definition and is correct, but exponential in n — useful only to build intuition or validate on tiny inputs.
s: Precompute cnt_i = number of j ≠ i with factor_i dividing factor_j.
Find the minimum price mn over all items.
For every subset S of types with total price ≤ budget, evaluate |S| + Σ cnt_i + (budget − cost) // mn.
a.t: O(2^n · n) — enumerating all subsets with linear evaluation per subset; only feasible for n ≲ 20.

a.i: Since the free bonus of a type is fixed once you own it, 'buying type i' is a one-time decision worth 1 + cnt_i at cost price_i. Run a standard 0/1 knapsack where dp[b] = best (copies + free bonus) using exactly at most b budget. Finally, for each achievable spend b, add floor((budget − b) / mn) extra copies bought with leftover money at the global minimum price — duplicates of already-owned types are dominated by this. The answer is the maximum over all b.
s: Compute cnt_i for every item via pairwise divisibility checks.
Let mn be the minimum price across all items.
For each item (price p, value 1 + cnt_i), update dp[b] = max(dp[b], dp[b−p] + value) iterating b downward (0/1 knapsack).
Answer = max over reachable b of dp[b] + (budget − b) // mn.
a.t: O(n^2 + n · budget) — O(n^2) pairwise divisibility precomputation dominates alongside the O(n · budget) knapsack; about 2.25 million operations at max constraints.
a.sp: O(n + budget) — the cnt array and 1D dp array.

w: In an interview, present the key reduction first — free copies depend only on the set of purchased types — then go straight to the knapsack DP; the brute force is mainly a sanity-check tool. Common pitfalls: (1) treating the problem as unbounded knapsack over copies and double-counting free bonuses — buying a second copy of a type adds no free copies; (2) forgetting that leftover money should buy the globally cheapest item, even one whose type was never 'activated'; (3) off-by-one when a type divides itself — exclude i = j in cnt; (4) unreachable dp states must be excluded before adding the leftover term. Edge cases: a single item, all identical factors (every purchase frees every other type), and budget smaller than every price (answer 0). Likely follow-ups: what if free copies also granted further free copies transitively (they don't here), or if buying k copies granted k free copies — both would push toward different DP formulations.
